extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, comparative government, and American history
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and analytical dimensions for judging the durability and strength of a federal/confederate union (why a Union holds together or disintegrates), as articulated in a 19th-century political analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderating force resides in the States rather than in the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: The preponderating force lies in the States rather than in the Union; provincial governments are more constantly felt and therefore attract the attachment of citizens more than the distant central government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: Federal undertakings are vast but rarely felt; provincial acts are small but incessant and affect individual welfare directly (liberty, property, daily life). The federal government is 'very far removed from its subjects' while provincial governments are 'within the reach of them all.' This closeness gives states greater practical influence over citizens' loyalties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Union endures only while States choose to remain members
rubrics_metrics.description: The Union will only last as long as all the States choose to belong to it — the Union was formed by the voluntary agreement of the States, who 'have not forfeited their nationality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: If a portion of the Union seriously desired separation, the Union could not easily prevent it; the question is whether States will choose to remain united rather than whether separation is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of governmental objects: national, provincial, mixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Some affairs are national by nature (war, diplomacy), some provincial (local budgets), and some mixed (civil and political rights) which may be regulated nationally or provincially according to the agreement of the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides allocation of powers: mixed affairs can be assigned either way without necessarily impairing the union; the way mixed affairs are allocated affects the balance of preponderance between center and provinces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of sovereignty determines tendency toward centralization or dismemberment
rubrics_metrics.description: When sovereign power is composed of individuals centralization tends to prevail; when formed by preorganized political bodies (states) confederations tend toward dismemberment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: Confederations composed of preexisting sovereignties cede only indispensable powers to the center, preserving strong provincial authority and making the national government weaker and prone to being stripped of necessary privileges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity and responsiveness of provincial governments strengthen them
rubrics_metrics.description: Provincial governments, being near citizens, can address even the smallest appeals and thus sustain continual authority, whereas the central government must parley and persuade when dealing with states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: State governments' clear, imperative language toward individuals contrasts with federal negotiation with States; this difference sustains state loyalty and weakens federal capacity to command states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical geography and population dispersion limit federal coercive power
rubrics_metrics.description: Vast territory, great distances, and a dispersed population make it difficult for the Union to enforce allegiance by military means; absence of standing armies reduces government's readiness to coerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and notes: United States' size likened to five times France; lack of natural barriers and scattered population (half a wilderness) compared to England during its War of Independence; translator's note and later historical events (Civil War) indicate some misprediction but principle explains difficulty of coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of natural barriers fosters unity if interests are not conflicting
rubrics_metrics.description: No natural barriers exist between the States (Alleghanies do not separate peoples); such openness facilitates interchange and, provided no contrary interests arise, the extent of territory may favor prosperity and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Qualification: Large territory is beneficial only insofar as inhabitants are not divided by opposing interests; contrary interests across vast areas can produce dissension and harm unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal material interests (commerce, production) bind different regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct regional economies (South agricultural; North commercial/manufacturing; West mixed) create reciprocal interests (raw materials, markets, fleets) that make the Union materially useful to all parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elaboration: North needs Southern/Western raw materials and consumers; South/West rely on Northern commerce and navy for export protection. Federal budget and fleet protect mutual material interests and thus encourage preservation of the Union.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immaterial ties: uniformity of opinions, shared political and moral beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Shared political, religious, moral, and philosophical opinions — e.g., belief that the people are the source of power, value of liberty, equality, press freedom, jury, and public opinion — create social unity beyond mere legal ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: Society endures when 'a great number of men consider a great number of things in the same point of view.' Public opinion and a common faith in progress/perfectibility unify citizens across states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different characters and passions among citizens threaten the Union
rubrics_metrics.description: Dangers arise not from diversity of interests per se but from differing characters and passions (e.g., effects of climate and slavery) that alter habits, manners, and temperaments between regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed example: Slavery in the South produces masters habituated to command (supercilious, irascible, ardent), whereas Northern self-reliance produces patience, tolerance, and perseverance — these character differences create social and political tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unequal dependence on the Union produces incentives to support or oppose central authority
rubrics_metrics.description: If some states exclusively enjoy principal advantages of union or their prosperity depends on it, they will support the central government in enforcing obedience; otherwise, because benefits are broadly distributed, no single state is likely to sacrifice greatly to maintain the Union.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: Federal power may derive force from unequal distribution of benefits, but such force is contrary to the nature of confederations; in the American case, the Union is advantageous but not indispensable to any single State.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preponderance of one state can convert the Union into an instrument of that state
rubrics_metrics.description: If one state obtains sufficient preponderance to take exclusive possession of central authority, the federal government may act as its instrument and the Union's nominal authority masks domination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical analogies: province of Holland in the Low Countries and the Emperor in the Germanic Confederation sometimes used federal authority for their own advantage; this undermines genuine federal institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public opinion and shared civic dispositions are essential for social existence
rubrics_metrics.description: A society exists not merely by obedience to laws but because many people hold similar opinions and feelings; the 'absolute moral authority of the reason of the community' and faith in public opinion bind citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: Common belief in popular sovereignty, equality, press and association rights, and belief in progress underpin the Anglo-American cohesion despite multiple sovereignties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Population movements and rapid growth shift power and create passions
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid expansion (progress of population to the Northwest) causes power to gravitate and may generate passions from sudden turns of fortune that threaten institutional stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: Growth changes demographics and political weight of regions, which can alter the balance of interests and produce emotional political reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material incentives against secession: lack of tangible benefit to leave
rubrics_metrics.description: It is almost impossible to discover material interests that would tempt a portion of the Union to separate at present; the temporal interests of different parts are intimately connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: Given the integrated commercial, naval, and political advantages, no obvious material motive exists to leave; thus secession is unlikely unless other forces (character differences, political changes) overcome material ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of mixed affairs affects balance of federal vs provincial power
rubrics_metrics.description: When the national government is invested with the right to regulate mixed affairs (partly general, partly local), it acquires preponderating influence because all rights it does not possess exist by its sufferance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: Granting national control over mixed matters can gradually strip provincial governments of prerogatives and concentrate power in the center; conversely, provincial control over mixed matters tends to keep preponderance with the states.
